t.site of luoyang city from the eastern ha:
Luoyang, in Henan province, is one of the four great ancient capitals of China, a city that served as the seat of more than a dozen dynasties over a thousand years. East of the modern city, in the fields along the Luo river, lie the remains of the capital of the Eastern Han dynasty, which ruled from Luoyang from the first to the early third century AD, and of the later Wei, Jin and Northern Wei capitals built on the same site. The site is part of the UNESCO-listed Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor, inscribed in 2014.

Little remains above ground: earthen walls, the foundations of palaces and gates, and the outlines of a city that once housed hundreds of thousands of people. Archaeologists have uncovered sections of the city walls and the remains of the imperial academy and the Lingtai observatory. The vast scale of the site, and the sense of history beneath the fields, is what impresses.

Nearby, the White Horse Temple is traditionally considered the first Buddhist temple in China, founded under the Eastern Han in the first century AD, when two Indian monks arrived with scriptures on white horses. South of the city, the Longmen Grottoes, a UNESCO site in their own right, contain tens of thousands of Buddhist statues carved into the limestone cliffs along the Yi river, from tiny figures to a giant Buddha seventeen metres high.

Riding in China as a foreigner is complicated. A Chinese driving licence is required, foreign vehicles need special permits and often a guide, and motorcycles are restricted or banned in the centres of many cities. If you are on an organised tour, the guide will handle the details. Traffic is heavy, with a mix of cars, trucks, electric scooters and pedestrians. The roads around Luoyang are mostly modern highways and busy urban roads.

Luoyang has every service. The city is famous for its peonies, celebrated in a festival in April, and for its water banquet, a series of soups and broths. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.longmen grottoes@34.5,112.5:
South of Luoyang, the river Yi cuts through a narrow gap between two limestone hills, and for about a kilometre the cliffs on both sides are honeycombed with caves, niches and carvings. Over around four centuries, starting in the late fifth century under the Northern Wei dynasty and continuing through the Tang, Buddhist sculptors carved tens of thousands of statues into the rock, from tiny figures a few centimetres high to colossal Buddhas. The Longmen Grottoes were listed by UNESCO in 2000 and are among the finest examples of Chinese Buddhist art.

The highlight is the Fengxian Temple, an open-air group of giant figures cut into the western cliff in the Tang period. At its centre sits a huge Vairocana Buddha, serene and majestic, flanked by disciples, bodhisattvas and fierce guardians. Tradition holds that its face was modelled on the Empress Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule China in her own name, who supported the project. Many smaller statues are missing heads, removed by looters and collectors in the early twentieth century, and some are now in museums abroad.

Luoyang was one of the great capitals of ancient China, and it is famous today for its peonies, which bloom in April during a large festival. The city's water banquet, a meal of many soups and stews served in succession, is a local tradition. A couple of hours east, on the slopes of Song Shan, stands the Shaolin Temple, birthplace of Zen Buddhism in China and of its famous martial arts.

On the practical side, getting around on two wheels is the hard part. Foreigners usually need a Chinese licence or a special permit to ride, motorbikes are banned from expressways, and many cities restrict their use in central areas. Most visitors reach Longmen by bus, taxi or high-speed train to Luoyang. Traffic in the city is dense and chaotic, with electric scooters weaving silently around you.

The best time to visit is early morning or late afternoon, when the light falls on the carvings and the crowds are thinner; in the evening, the cliffs are lit up, reflected in the river. Fuel, food and every service are available in Luoyang. Try a bowl of spicy beef soup with flatbread, a local breakfast favourite.
t.site of dingding@34.6,112.5:
Luoyang was a capital for so many Chinese dynasties that locals like to say it holds the history of thirteen of them, and the Dingding Gate was the grand southern entrance of the outer city in the Sui and Tang periods, when Luoyang was one of the largest cities in the world. Through it passed officials, merchants, pilgrims and ambassadors, many of them travelling on the routes that linked China with Central Asia and beyond, which is why it forms part of the UNESCO listing of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor, inscribed in 2014. Excavations revealed the foundations of the gate and the road surface, with ruts and even footprints of people and animals, now protected inside a modern museum building that echoes the shape of the original gate.

Luoyang has more to offer than most cities its size. The Longmen Grottoes, south of the city, contain tens of thousands of Buddha statues carved into the limestone cliffs along the Yi river, also listed by UNESCO, and the White Horse Temple, east of the city, is traditionally regarded as the first Buddhist temple in China. The Shaolin Temple, famous for kung fu, lies in the Song mountains about an hour's ride to the south-east.

Riding in and around Luoyang means busy urban traffic, wide boulevards, electric scooters everywhere and drivers with their own interpretation of lanes. As elsewhere in China, foreign riders need local permits and licences, and some roads restrict motorcycles. Outside the city, roads into the Song mountains and toward the Yellow River offer more interesting riding, with hills, river valleys and villages.

Fuel, food and every service are easy to find in a city of more than a million people. Luoyang is famous for its water banquet, a series of soups and broths served in a set order, and for its peonies, which bloom in April and attract huge crowds to the peony festival. Street food includes beef soup with flatbread, noodles and dumplings.

Come in April for the peonies, or in autumn for clear skies and comfortable temperatures. Summer is hot and humid, winter cold. The ruts in the old road surface, worn by cartwheels more than a thousand years ago, are the detail that stays with you long after the grand reconstructions fade.
t.architectural complex of shaolin temple@:
Ask most people where kung fu comes from and they will name this temple, even if they have no idea where it is. The Shaolin Temple stands at the foot of Mount Song in Henan province, central China, near the city of Dengfeng. It was founded at the end of the fifth century for an Indian monk, and tradition says that Bodhidharma, the legendary founder of Chan, or Zen, Buddhism, meditated in a cave on the mountain above for nine years. The monks' martial arts became famous over the centuries, and today Shaolin is as much a brand as a monastery.

The temple complex includes halls, courtyards, ancient trees and the Pagoda Forest, a remarkable collection of hundreds of brick and stone tomb pagodas of eminent monks, built over more than a thousand years. Together with other buildings around Dengfeng, including an ancient academy and an astronomical observatory, it was inscribed in 2010 as the Historic Monuments of Dengfeng in the Centre of Heaven and Earth. The area around the temple is full of martial arts schools, and you will see thousands of students training in the open air.

Mount Song is one of the five sacred mountains of China, a range of steep, rocky peaks with temples, paths and cable cars. The scenery is dramatic, with cliffs, forests and views over the plain. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, as summers are hot and humid and winters cold and dry.

Riding in China requires preparation. Foreigners need a Chinese licence or a temporary permit, and bringing a foreign bike usually requires an agency and a guide. Motorcycles are banned or restricted in many cities, and highway access for bikes varies. In the countryside of Henan, roads range from modern highways to narrow village lanes, with heavy traffic, trucks and electric scooters everywhere.

Songyang, part of Dengfeng and ten kilometres away, is where to find fuel, beds and a bowl of noodles. Henan's food is hearty and wheat-based: noodles, steamed buns and the famous Henan hui mian, a stewed noodle dish. The Longmen Grottoes, with their thousands of Buddhist carvings, are a couple of hours west near Luoyang and make a natural companion trip.
t.mendut temple@-7.6,110.2:
Mendut is the small, elegant temple that most visitors pass on their way to Borobudur, and that is a mistake. Built in the early ninth century under the Sailendra dynasty, it stands about three kilometres east of the great monument, on a straight line that also passes through the tiny Pawon temple, and scholars believe the three were connected in a ritual sequence. Each year, at the Buddhist festival of Waisak, monks walk in procession from Mendut through Pawon to Borobudur, carrying candles and chanting.

The temple itself is a square stone building on a high platform, with walls carved with reliefs of Buddhist deities and scenes from fables. The real treasure is inside. In a dim chamber sit three huge stone figures: a seated Buddha, his hands in the gesture of teaching, flanked by the bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Vajrapani. They are among the finest Buddhist sculptures in Southeast Asia, serene and powerful, and the cool darkness of the chamber after the bright sunshine outside makes the encounter almost startling. Next door is a Buddhist monastery, still active, with gardens where you can sit in the shade.

The landscape is the volcanic heart of Central Java. Rice paddies, coconut palms and villages fill the plain of the Progo and Elo rivers, and the cone of Mount Merapi, one of the most active volcanoes in Indonesia, rises to the east, often smoking. To the west, the Menoreh hills form a green wall. Early morning is the best time, when the air is clear, the volcanoes are visible, and the light on the paddies is soft.

Riding in Java is an adventure. Traffic drives on the left, and the roads are crowded with motorcycles, scooters, trucks and buses, all following their own logic. Overtaking is constant, the horn is a form of communication, and patience is essential. The roads around Borobudur and Mendut are smaller and calmer, winding through villages and paddies, but watch for chickens, children and potholes. The heat and humidity are intense, and afternoon downpours are common in the rainy season, roughly from November to March.

Muntilan, seven kilometres away, has fuel, and so do the villages around Borobudur, where small roadside stalls sell petrol in bottles. Magelang and Yogyakarta are the larger towns. Eat at a warung: a plate of nasi goreng and a sweet iced tea will put you right.
t.shaoshi que gates@34.5,113.0:
A que is a gate tower, and the Shaoshi Que is a pair of them, standing like two stone gateposts at the foot of Mount Shaoshi in Henan province, on the approach to the sacred mountain. They date from the Han dynasty, nearly two thousand years ago, and are among the oldest surviving examples of this type of monument in China. The tall stone shafts, with carved reliefs of hunting scenes, animals and chariots, stand on the slope with the mountain behind them. Together with the Taishi and Qimu que on neighbouring mountains, they belong to the group of monuments in Dengfeng that UNESCO recognised in 2010 as the Centre of Heaven and Earth.

The mountain is part of the sacred Mount Song, one of China's five great peaks, which has been a religious and political centre for millennia. Early Chinese rulers saw this region as the middle of the world, and Taoist, Buddhist and Confucian traditions all left their mark. Just up the valley is the Shaolin Temple, the monastery that is the legendary birthplace of Chan Buddhism and a famous home of martial arts, which draws crowds of visitors and performers.

The countryside around Dengfeng is dry, hilly farmland, with orchards and walnut trees, and the limestone and sandstone mountains rise abruptly from the plain. Songyang, with about 60,000 people only six kilometres away, is the main place for supplies, and Zhengzhou, the provincial capital, is to the east. Roads are good, with expressways and well-surfaced local routes, though traffic and trucks can be heavy. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summers are hot and winters can be bitterly cold and dry.

As with any plan for China, check how motorcycles are treated. Foreign licences are not valid on Chinese roads, temporary permits are complicated to arrange, and many city centres restrict motorcycles. Most visitors will take a taxi or a local bus to the site. The mountain air, the sound of wind in the pines and the rows of old stone make the stop worth the effort. Local food in Henan leans on wheat, so expect hand-pulled noodles and steamed buns, with a spicy kick in many dishes.
t.observatory@34.4,113.1:
The oldest surviving observatory in China sits in an unassuming spot in Dengfeng, in Henan, and it makes astronomy look more like architecture. The Gaocheng Astronomical Observatory was built in 1276 under the Yuan dynasty by the astronomer Guo Shoujing, who designed a stout stone tower about 9 metres high with a long stone scale running north from its base. The tower was a giant gnomon: the sun cast a shadow along the scale, and by measuring its length at noon through the year, the astronomers could fix the solstices and the length of the year with remarkable accuracy. The calendar that Guo helped create was in use for several centuries.

The site is older than the tower, because this part of Henan was considered the centre of the world, and a much earlier gnomon here is credited to the Duke of Zhou, a figure from over three thousand years ago. The observatory forms part of the Dengfeng group on the UNESCO list, along with the Shaolin Temple's pagoda forest, the Songyang Academy and the Han que gates. It is a good reminder that Chinese science and religion were intertwined with ideas of order and the cosmos.

You will find the countryside dry and open, with wheat fields, walnut trees and the bare ridges of Mount Song to the north. Songyang, a town of about 60,000 people 12 km away, has fuel, food and hotels. The roads are good, though trucks and local traffic make riding a slog at times. Foreign riders should check carefully on licensing before planning to ride in China, since regulations are strict and enforcement is firm.

Spring and autumn are best, and clear winter days can be sharp and bright. Take a moment at the tower to look at how the shadow falls, and read the small museum signs if you can. The temperature on the plateau drops sharply at night, and in summer the afternoon heat is considerable. Henan food is built around wheat, so a bowl of hand-pulled noodles or a steamed bun filled with pork will refuel you better than a snack bar. The best light for photographs is late afternoon, when the stone glows warm.
t.mosquee de kouto@9.9,-6.4:
Kouto is a small town in the far north of Côte d'Ivoire, close to the borders with Mali and Burkina Faso, and its mosque is one of the best-known of the Sudanese-style buildings of the region. Mud-brick walls rise in battered buttresses, each topped by a small pinnacle, and timber beams project from the surface like the quills of a hedgehog. Seen across a field in the morning light, it looks as though it grew there.

Take a moment to think about how this landscape looks from a motorbike. The country around Kouto is open savanna, with shea trees, mango groves, cashew plantations and cotton or maize fields, and low granite hills here and there. The road surface can be good on main routes and rough on the side roads, with laterite dust in the dry season and mud when the rains come. Between December and February the harmattan blows in from the Sahara, dimming the sun and coating everything in fine dust, which is a nuisance for riders but turns sunsets a deep red.

The tradition behind the mosques is tied to Dyula traders, Muslim merchants who moved goods like kola nuts, gold and salt across West Africa. They founded commercial towns, and the mosque was the centre of each one. Over time local masons developed the Sudanese style, using the same earth as the houses and the same techniques, and the rebuilding of the plaster after the rains became a village event. Some mosques here are several centuries old in their foundations, even though the surface is renewed every year.

There is no sizeable town on the list, and services can be thin. Plan fuel in advance, because stations are not frequent in the north, and carry water and cash in small notes. Use local help to find the right person to ask for access, and be modest in dress. The people in the villages are friendly, curious and used to visitors who stop for a few minutes and take photographs. Respect for the building and for the people who maintain it makes the stop worthwhile.
t.site of shihao section of xiaohan ancien:
The Silk Road is often imagined as a line across a desert, but in places it was a road cut into rock. The Xiaohan ancient road runs through the mountains of Henan province, linking Luoyang, the Han and Tang capital, with the west through the narrow pass at Hangu. The Shihao section is a stretch of the road that survives in the loess hills, with ruts cut into the stone by wheels. UNESCO listed it as part of the Silk Roads network in 2014.

The road was used from the Han dynasty onwards, more than two thousand years ago, and it was the main route between the central plain and Chang'an, now Xi'an. Carts, mules and soldiers climbed this pass for centuries. The ruts in the stone, worn deep by wheels, show how heavy the traffic was. The terrain is steep and broken, with narrow valleys and yellow cliffs of windblown silt, and it can be hard to imagine a road through it. Yet people kept using it, because there was no easy alternative.

The landscape is the loess plateau, a land of fine yellow soil that the wind carried from the deserts in the northwest over millions of years. It erodes into deep gullies and terraces, and farmers have carved cave houses into the cliffs. Fields of wheat and corn cling to the slopes, and in spring the orchards bloom. The roads wind through the gullies, and the weather can be dry and dusty or wet and slippery.

There is no sizeable town near the site, and Yima, thirty-four kilometres away, is the nearest place of any size, with about eighty thousand people. Plan fuel and food accordingly. In China, riding a foreign motorcycle is generally not allowed without local registration, so check before you plan a trip. If you come on foot or by car, wear sturdy shoes, because the ground is rough, and bring water. In autumn the hills turn gold, and the evening light on the loess cliffs is warm.
t.no 160 site of hanjia granary@34.7,112.5:
Luoyang was the capital of thirteen dynasties, and its history runs through the ground like a seam of coal. On the edge of the modern city, the Hanjia Granary is one of the biggest ancient grain stores ever found. It was built in the Sui dynasty, in the early seventh century, and used through the Tang, and the site has hundreds of underground storage pits, each one large enough to hold hundreds of tonnes of grain. UNESCO listed it as part of the Silk Roads in 2014.

Grain was power. The Sui and Tang emperors needed to feed their capital, their officials and their armies, and they built storehouses along the Grand Canal and the Luo river to collect grain from the south. Pit number 160, the one that gives the site its name, was excavated in the 1970s, and archaeologists found the remains of millet, still recognisable after more than a thousand years. The storage pits were lined with wood, straw and clay to keep out damp, and some of the bricks carry inscriptions telling where the grain came from and how much was stored.

Luoyang has about one and a half million people and sits in a wide valley of the Luo river, with mountains to the south. It is famous for peonies, which bloom in April and fill the city with festival crowds. The Longmen Grottoes, a cliff of Buddhist carvings a few kilometres south, are among the finest monuments of Chinese art, and the White Horse Temple, said to be the first Buddhist temple in China, is nearby. The local food is excellent, including the water banquet, a series of soups served in sequence.

As in the rest of China, riding a motorcycle as a foreigner is complicated, so check the rules. Luoyang has fuel, hotels and restaurants on every street, and the traffic can be heavy. April is the peony season and a lovely time to come, but also very busy. Autumn is calm and clear. Take an hour at the granary to walk along the pits and imagine the carts arriving.
t.qimu que gates@34.5,113.0:
In the Han dynasty, important places were marked with gate towers called que, tall pairs of stone pillars with carved roofs, set in front of tombs, temples and palaces. Only a few dozen survive in China, and three of them stand at the foot of Mount Song, in Henan. The Qimu Que, the gate of Lady Qimu, named for the mother of Qi, son of the legendary Yu of the Xia dynasty, is one of the group, and it stands in front of a temple that no longer exists. They date from the second century AD, about nineteen hundred years ago.

The stone gate carries relief carvings of horses, chariots, dancers and animals, in a lively, fluid style, and you can see how the carvers imitated wooden architecture in stone. Mount Song is one of the five sacred mountains of China, and the region around Dengfeng was thought to be the centre of the world, which is why UNESCO listed the historic monuments of Dengfeng in 2010. Nearby are the Zhongyue Temple, the Songyang Academy, the Shaolin Temple, famous for its martial arts, and an old observatory dating from the Yuan dynasty.

The landscape is stony, with steep limestone ridges, terraces and small orchards, and it is quite different from the flat plain further east. Roads climb gently towards the foothills, with long views to the ridge of Mount Song. The weather is moderate, with cold winters and warm, wet summers, and the best seasons are spring and autumn. The area is busy at weekends and holidays, when tour buses fill the roads.

Songyang is a small town only a couple of kilometres away, with about sixty thousand people, and Dengfeng nearby has fuel, restaurants and hotels. Try the local noodles and the steamed buns, and drink the tea. Riders from abroad should remember that riding a motorcycle in China usually requires local registration, so make sure you know the rules. Early morning is quiet, and the stones look their best in raking light.
t.site of huiloa granary@34.7,112.5:
Huiluo Granary was the pantry of the Sui dynasty, and the scale of it is hard to take in. Built around 606, during the reign of Emperor Yang, on a rise northeast of the new eastern capital of Luoyang, it was one of the great state storehouses along the Grand Canal, designed to hold grain shipped in from the rich lands of the east and south. The Sui emperors dug canals at a furious pace to link the Yellow and Yangtze basins, and granaries like this one were the stockpiles that kept the capital, the army and the court fed.

Archaeologists have found hundreds of underground storage pits here, big circular cellars dug into the loess soil and lined to keep out damp, laid out in neat rows inside a walled compound. Some of the pits held remains of grain, and charred millet has been found, a sign of fire or decay in the final days. The Sui dynasty collapsed in 618, partly because of the cost of such projects, and the grain stores were fought over in the civil wars that followed. The granary site was included in the Grand Canal's UNESCO listing in 2014.

On the ground, expect an excavated field with protective structures over some pits, boards explaining the work in Chinese, and wide skies. It is not decorative, but a good place to understand the logistics behind imperial China. Luoyang, one of the ancient capitals of China and only five kilometres away, has far more to see, including the Longmen Grottoes, with thousands of Buddhist carvings, the White Horse Temple and a famous peony festival in April.

The roads around Luoyang are busy, with trucks, buses and scooters, and the ride to Zhengzhou along the Yellow River plain is long and flat. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and summer can be sweltering. Luoyang is a big city, with plenty of fuel, workshops and hotels, and a local speciality, the Luoyang water banquet, a set of dishes served as soups. Check the rules for foreign motorcyclists in China well before you plan a trip.
t.zhengzhou section of tongji canal@34.9,1:
Zhengzhou is a modern city of over four million people built on top of a very old one. Under the streets lie the walls of a Shang dynasty city some three and a half thousand years old, parts of which are still visible as long banks of rammed earth, and the Yellow River runs just north of town. The city is the capital of Henan, the province that some Chinese call the cradle of civilisation, and for much of history the plains around here were the political centre of the country.

The Tongji Canal ran through this region in the Sui dynasty, linking the Yellow River at the east end of the Luoyang area with the Huai River in the south-east. Under Emperor Yang, who ordered it built in the early seventh century, millions of labourers were drafted for the work, and the cost in lives contributed to the fall of the dynasty. Yet the canal outlived the dynasty that dug it, carrying southern rice and silk to the northern capitals for centuries. The Zhengzhou section is a modest survivor, a stretch of excavated bank and water kept as a heritage site, listed as part of the Grand Canal in 2014.

For the rider, central Henan is a flat world of wheat fields, brick villages and busy roads. Highways here are wide and fast, with heavy lorry traffic, and local roads are narrower and rougher. Beautiful riding lies to the west, where the Song mountains rise above the plain and the Shaolin Temple, the cradle of Chinese kung fu, stands in a wooded valley. Roads climb into the hills with a series of bends and tunnels, and the scenery changes from farmland to forested ridges.

Fuel is easy to find in and around the city, and food is hearty and filling, with hand-pulled noodles, braised lamb and the local specialty of Henan, a soup of wheat and spices known as hulatang. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with mild temperatures, and the dust and smog of winter can be unpleasant. In summer, heavy rain can come with little warning, and in 2021 the city suffered devastating floods. Foreign riders in China face strict rules about licences, plates and guides, so check the situation before you plan a ride.
t.geraldton@-28.8,114.6:
Geraldton sits on Champion Bay, about four hundred kilometres north of Perth, and it is the largest city on the Coral Coast, with more than twenty-six thousand people. It has a deep working harbour, long white beaches and a stiff southerly wind that makes it a magnet for windsurfers and kitesurfers, who flock to the beaches near the city in summer. The air smells of salt and diesel, and the light is brilliant.

The city's economy is built on rock lobster, locally called crayfish, and the fishing fleet works the Houtman Abrolhos Islands, a coral archipelago about sixty kilometres offshore. These islands hold a grim piece of history: in 1629 the Dutch ship Batavia was wrecked on the reefs, and the survivors suffered a terrible mutiny and massacre. The shipwreck museum in Geraldton and the Western Australian Museum tell the story with real artefacts. On a hill above the city stands the memorial to HMAS Sydney, lost with all hands in a battle with a German raider in 1941, a quiet, moving place with a view across the bay.

The cathedral of St Francis Xavier, designed by the priest and architect John Hawes in the early twentieth century, is a striking piece of Spanish mission style with domes and arches, and an unexpected sight in a Western Australian port. Geraldton has all the services a rider needs, with many fuel stations, supermarkets, cafes and fish and chip shops, and it is the last big town before the long, sparsely populated run north.

Top the tank here before heading north to Kalbarri and Shark Bay, because distances between towns are long. The road north follows the coast closely at first, with sand dunes, limestone cliffs and wide views, and in spring the roadside bursts with wildflowers. Winds can be strong, particularly in the afternoon, so keep a firm grip. In summer, temperatures can be fierce, so start early and carry water.
t.kalbarri@-27.7,114.2:
Kalbarri is a small town on the mouth of the Murchison River, where the river meets the Indian Ocean, and it is the gateway to a national park of the same name. The park covers a huge area of sandstone plateau, cut by deep gorges that expose layers of red and white rock laid down hundreds of millions of years ago. Lookouts such as Nature's Window, a natural arch framing the river below, and the Z Bend, where the gorge folds back on itself, are the main attractions, and the Skywalk platforms stick out into the void for those with a head for heights.

The town has around two and a half thousand people and a welcoming, beach-holiday feel. The estuary is a good place for swimming and paddling, and pelicans are fed on the foreshore each morning, drawing a crowd. Fuel, food and accommodation are all available, and there are cafes serving fresh fish, though prices rise in school holidays. South of town, the Zuytdorp Cliffs, where a Dutch ship of that name was wrecked in 1712, run along the coast for miles, and the sea crashes against them with great force.

The road from the highway to Kalbarri is a long spur of about sixty kilometres, and the wind can be strong, so be prepared for a fight with the weather. In spring, from August to October, the wildflowers bloom across the sandplains in a riot of colour, and the whole region is at its best. Summer is hot, very hot, and gorge walks are best done at dawn, with plenty of water.

Wildlife includes kangaroos, emus and a rich bird life, particularly around the river and the wetlands. At dusk, take care on the roads, because kangaroos are active and unpredictable. The ocean is beautiful but rips and currents can be dangerous, so swim only at patrolled or protected spots. After a day of riding, a cold drink and a sunset over the water are hard to beat.
t.malang@-8.0,112.6:
Malang is a cool, hilly city in East Java, at about 450 metres, and the altitude is the thing everyone mentions. After the heat of Surabaya, a couple of hours to the north, the evening air is a relief, and for the Dutch it was a favourite hill station, laid out in the early twentieth century with broad avenues, big trees and neat colonial villas around the central square. Some of that has survived, and the old streets near the Tugu monument still have a faded charm, though the city is now large and busy, with a university population and a lot of motorbikes.

The region has a long past. Just north of the city, at Singosari, a small stone temple, Candi Singosari, survives from the thirteenth-century kingdom of Singhasari, which was a forerunner of the great Majapahit empire. The surrounding hills are covered with orchards, and the town of Batu nearby is known for apples and strawberries, sold along the roadside in baskets. Food is a pleasure: bakso Malang, meatball soup with noodles and fried dumplings, is the city's pride, and tempeh and fried tofu are served at every stall.

Malang is also the starting point for the best-known road on the island, the way up to the Bromo Tengger Semeru national park. Mount Bromo, a smoking cone in a huge sandy caldera, is a few hours away, and the road from Tumpang climbs through villages and vegetable terraces to the crater rim, where jeeps carry people at three in the morning to catch the sunrise. Mount Semeru, the highest peak on Java, sometimes erupts in the distance. The road is steep and twisty, with tight hairpins, mist and sometimes rough patches, and the cold at dawn is serious, so dress in layers.

Traffic in town is dense, with scooters filling every gap, so allow extra time and keep your speed gentle. Fuel stations are everywhere, in a city of over seven hundred thousand people, and you will find plenty of small warung for rice, noodles and strong, sweet coffee. Many guesthouses have space for bikes, and parking attendants will guard your machine for a small tip. Leave early and you will be rewarded with the best of the day.
t.tumpang@-8.0,112.8:
Tumpang is a busy market town at the eastern edge of the Malang plain, in the heart of East Java, and for most visitors it is the place where the road to Mount Bromo begins. The town is where the highway from Malang squeezes through a bottleneck of shops, stalls and minibuses, and where the jeeps wait that take travellers up to the volcanoes. Behind it, the Tengger mountains rise in blue ridges, with the smoking cone of Semeru, the highest peak on Java, hovering above on a clear day.

Though it is easy to pass through quickly, the area has deep roots. In the thirteenth century this was the heartland of the Singhasari kingdom, one of the great Javanese empires before Majapahit, and temple ruins from that age still stand near Tumpang. Candi Jago, a stepped temple with carved reliefs, tells stories from Hindu and Buddhist traditions, and Candi Kidal, a few kilometres away, is a slender, elegant tower with a carving of Garuda, the mythical bird. Both are quiet places, often with nobody else there, and they give a quick glimpse of the long history behind the volcanic scenery.

Riding here is an exercise in Javanese traffic. The road from Malang, about fourteen kilometres away, is crowded with trucks, buses, angkot minibuses and scooters, with little regard for lanes, and the speed is slow. The roads into the highlands are narrower and steeper, but the surface is mostly good, and the air cools as you climb through villages, vegetable fields and pine forests. Early morning is the best time to start, to reach the highlands before the mist and afternoon rain, and the dry season, from May to October, is easier. Cold air at altitude means a jacket is essential for the early start.

The countryside around Tumpang is fertile, thanks to the volcanic soil, and it is covered in plots of cabbage, potatoes, onions and apples, tended by farmers in conical hats. Malang itself is known for its apples, tempeh chips and cooler climate, a favourite hill city of Dutch colonial times, with a handsome old centre.

Fuel is easy to find. Malang, with a population of well over seven hundred thousand, has stations everywhere, and Tumpang itself has several. Warungs along the main street serve soto, a spicy soup, and bakso, meatball soup, with sweet tea and coffee. Fill up in town before heading to the highlands, where stations are sparse.
t.jemplang@-8.0,112.9:
Jemplang is the place where the earth gives way. The road from Tumpang climbs through villages and pine forest to a rim at about 2,400 metres, and suddenly the whole Tengger caldera opens below: a flat, grey floor of volcanic sand, ten kilometres across, with the cones of Bromo and Batok rising from it like toys on a tray, and beyond them, the great symmetrical bulk of Semeru, the highest mountain on Java at 3,676 metres, puffing a plume of ash every twenty minutes or so. It is one of the most startling views in Indonesia, and it takes a moment to understand the scale.

From the viewpoint, a track descends to the Sea of Sand, or Segara Wedi, a vast ash plain where jeeps bounce across the grey, and to the green hills that tourists have nicknamed the Teletubbies hills, a series of smooth, grassy folds covered in savannah. In the wet season, they are an intense green, and in the dry season, a pale gold. The caldera is protected as the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, and the Tengger people, a Hindu minority descended from the Majapahit empire, live in villages on its slopes and farm vegetables on impossibly steep plots.

The Tumpang approach is a real mountain road. Beyond the last villages, the surface becomes narrower and rougher, with tight bends and steep gradients, and the air gets cold. Fog and drizzle are common, and rain can turn the surface greasy. Dawn and early morning bring the clearest views before the clouds roll in. The dry season, from about May to October, is the best time. Rules for private vehicles on the caldera floor have changed over the years, and the park charges entry fees and sets limits on access, so ask at Tumpang or at the park office before you plan to ride down onto the sand, and expect that jeeps may be required.

The Tengger celebrate a festival called Yadnya Kasada each year, when they carry offerings of rice, fruit, vegetables and livestock to the crater rim of Bromo and throw them into the abyss. It is a remarkable ceremony, and the mountain is sacred to them.

Simple warungs near the rim sell hot tea, instant noodles and fried bananas, welcome in the cold. Wear gloves and a windproof jacket, and carry a scarf or mask for the dust and sulphur in the air.
t.mount bromo viewpoint@-7.9,112.9:
Bromo is not the tallest peak in the Tengger caldera, but it is the one that smokes, and nobody who sees it forgets it. The crater, at 2,329 metres, sits in the middle of a plain of grey volcanic sand, with a steady plume of white sulphurous steam rising from its throat, and the smell of rotten eggs drifting down the slope. To the south, the neat cone of Batok, covered in green ridges, stands beside it, and behind them both, Semeru, bigger and often more active, sends up puffs of ash. The whole scene looks like an illustration from a children's book about volcanoes.

The most famous viewpoint, Penanjakan, is on the caldera rim at about 2,770 metres, and it draws a long queue of jeeps long before dawn. From there, at first light, you look down on a sea of cloud with the volcanoes rising from it like islands, and the sun comes up in a band of orange behind Semeru. It is cold, crowded and magnificent, and getting there at 3 or 4 in the morning is part of the ritual. Come prepared with a down jacket, gloves and a hat, since temperatures near freezing are not unusual.

Riding here requires care. The roads up to the rim from Pasuruan or Probolinggo are steep and winding, with hairpins and poor visibility in fog, and in the dark, the traffic of jeeps and motorcycles can be thick. The surface is mostly sealed, but patched and rough in places, and sand and gravel drift onto the bends. Many riders leave the bike below and take a jeep, since the final approach and the access to the sand sea are restricted and rules change from time to time, so ask locally. The dry season, May to October, gives the clearest skies, and the wet season brings fog and rain.

At the foot of Bromo, a Hindu temple, Pura Luhur Poten, stands on the sand, where the Tengger community, who have kept the Hindu faith since the fall of Majapahit, make offerings. Steps lead up to the crater rim, which can be climbed in about twenty minutes, and the sulphur fumes are strong, so a mask is useful.

Fuel stations are found in the lowland towns such as Lawang, Pasuruan and Probolinggo, and small stalls in the highland villages sell petrol, but supplies are limited, so fill up before the climb. Small warungs near the rim serve hot coffee and noodles, and a sweet, hot ginger tea is a welcome comfort in the dawn chill.
t.cemoro lawang@-7.9,113.0:
Cemoro Lawang sits on the rim of the Tengger caldera in East Java, and the view from the village edge is one of the strangest in the tropics. Below you lies a vast, flat sea of grey volcanic sand, and out of it rise the cones of Bromo, with its smoking crater, and Semeru beyond, the highest peak on Java. The village is high, cold at night and wrapped in mist at dawn, and everything about it feels a long way from the sweaty lowlands you left. Pasuruan and Lawang are the nearest big towns, around thirty kilometres away and a long climb below.

The Tengger people who live here are a Hindu community in a mostly Muslim island, and they hold the mountain sacred. Each year at the Yadnya Kasada festival, they climb to the crater and throw offerings, vegetables, flowers and livestock, into it. You will see small shrines and offerings on the slopes and men in sarongs against the cold. The caldera floor is called the Sea of Sand, and vehicles cross it in the dark so that visitors can reach the viewpoint for sunrise.

The ride up is the point. The road climbs steeply through market gardens where farmers grow cabbages, potatoes and onions on slopes that look too steep for anything, and the air cools with every bend. Expect tight hairpins, patchy tarmac, motorbikes loaded with sacks, minibuses taking corners wide, and plenty of morning mist. Ride slowly, because the fog comes quickly and the drops are real. Nights are cold enough for a proper jacket, which surprises people who packed for the tropics.

Bring fuel from the lowlands, as the village is small and roadside bottles of petrol are the usual fallback rather than a station. There are simple guesthouses and warung serving fried rice, noodles and strong coffee, and the ash dust gets into everything, so a buff or mask is wise. The best time is the dry season, from roughly May to September, when sunrises are clear. Set an alarm for the middle of the night, because the view is worth the dark start.
t.chita@52.0,113.5:
Chita has the odd distinction of being both a big city and a place that feels like the edge of the world. With about 300,000 people, it is the capital of Zabaykalsky Krai and sits in a bowl of hills where the Chita and Ingoda rivers meet, beyond Lake Baikal and well before the Pacific. It began in the seventeenth century as a Cossack outpost, grew with the arrival of the Trans-Siberian Railway around the turn of the twentieth century, and became widely known earlier as a place of exile. Several Decembrist officers, who had led an uprising against the tsar in 1825, were sent here, and their presence left a mark of learning and culture in a town that might otherwise have remained a frontier camp.

For a rider arriving from the west, Chita is the first real city after a long run of taiga and steppe, and it offers everything you may want: fuel stations on every main road, large supermarkets, cafes serving everything from Buryat dumplings to burgers, hotels of every grade and mechanics who have seen plenty of tired bikes. The streets can be busy at rush hour, and the cobbled and patched pavement of older districts is rough, but the centre is easy to find and the setting is pleasant.

South and east of the city, the road toward the Dauria steppe is a different story. The highway crosses rolling grassland, with long gentle rises and wide, open views. Wind is common, and summer thunderstorms can be violent, with brief, heavy rain. Winters are bitterly cold and dry, with hard frost from November to March, so the riding season is short, running from late May to early September. July and August bring warmth, and the grass turns green and then gold across the hills.

Take time for the centre. The old Decembrist church and the museum devoted to the exiles are worth a short visit, and the cathedral and the main square show the confidence of a provincial capital that has always had to manage on its own. Local food leans on meat, dumplings and Siberian pelmeni, and you can find surprisingly good coffee near the main street. Fill the tank before heading out, because the steppe villages are small and the distances long.
t.the cosmological axis of yogyakarta and:
Yogyakarta was laid out along a line. In the eighteenth century, Sultan Hamengkubuwono I founded the city on an axis running from the smoking cone of Mount Merapi in the north to the Indian Ocean in the south, with the Tugu monument, the Kraton palace and the Panggung Krapyak stage pavilion placed along it, embodying Javanese ideas about the cycle of life and the relation between people, ruler and the cosmos. The Cosmological Axis of Yogyakarta and its Historic Landmarks was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2023, and the sultanate still functions: the sultan is also the governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta.

The Kraton, the sultan's palace, is a complex of pavilions, courtyards and museums, with performances of gamelan music, dance and wayang shadow puppetry on certain days. Jalan Malioboro, the busy street running north from the palace along the axis, is lined with shops and street vendors selling batik, leather and food late into the night. Taman Sari, the old water castle, with its bathing pools and underground passages, is a short walk from the Kraton.

Yogyakarta is a city of motorbikes, with hundreds of thousands of scooters swarming the streets, so riding here is about patience, flow and alertness. Traffic moves on the left, intersections are chaotic, and the rule is to go steadily and predictably. International riders need a valid licence, and helmets are mandatory. Fuel is everywhere, from Pertamina stations to roadside stalls selling petrol in bottles.

Beyond the city, the riding is excellent. The roads up the slopes of Merapi, an active volcano, lead to viewpoints and villages rebuilt after the eruption of 2010. To the north-west lies Borobudur, the great Buddhist monument, and to the east, Prambanan, the Hindu temple complex, both UNESCO sites. South, the roads lead to the coast at Parangtritis, a black-sand beach with strong currents and legends of the sea queen Nyi Roro Kidul. Try gudeg, the jackfruit stew that is Yogyakarta's signature dish, and ride early before the heat and rain of the afternoon.
t.the grand canal@34.7,112.5:
Luoyang is one of China's ancient capitals, a city with over a thousand years of imperial history pressed into its soil, and the Grand Canal is part of the reason why. In the early seventh century the Sui emperor Yang ordered a system of canals dug to link the Yellow River plain with the rice country of the south, and Luoyang became its great hub. Grain from the Yangtze delta was shipped here and stored in enormous underground granaries; one of them, the Hanjia granary inside the city, is part of the UNESCO listing of the Grand Canal and you can see the excavated grain pits today.

Standing beside the Luo river, it takes some effort to picture the barges and warehouses, because modern Luoyang is a sprawling city of more than a million people with wide avenues and towering apartment blocks. Yet the history pops up everywhere. South of town, the Longmen Grottoes line the Yi river with thousands of Buddhist carvings, including a giant Buddha that is said to bear the features of Empress Wu Zetian. In April the city celebrates its peony festival, and its parks fill with crowds photographing flowers the size of dinner plates. Local food includes the water banquet, a long sequence of soups and broths served in a strict order.

Riding here comes with practical limits. Foreign travellers generally need special permits and often a guide to ride their own motorcycle in China, and many city centres, Luoyang included, restrict or ban motorcycles on major roads. Expressways are closed to motorbikes. If you are on two wheels, the best riding is out on the provincial roads west towards the Han'gu Pass and east to Song Shan and the Shaolin Temple, where the loess hills fold into terraces and the traffic thins out.

Fuel is plentiful, and electric scooters outnumber petrol bikes by a wide margin. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer is humid and hot, winters dry and cold with occasional smog. Carry water and cash as backup, though mobile payment is nearly universal, and expect curious onlookers wherever you park a big touring bike.
t.prambanan temple compounds@-7.8,110.5:
Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia, a cluster of soaring stone towers on the plain between Yogyakarta and Solo, with the volcano Merapi brooding to the north. The central shrines were built in the ninth century and dedicated to the Trimurti: Shiva in the tallest tower, about forty-seven metres high, flanked by Brahma and Vishnu, with smaller temples for their mounts facing them. The walls are covered with reliefs of the Ramayana, carved so that you read the story as you walk clockwise around the galleries.

The site's history is a tale of collapse and rebuilding. Abandoned, shaken by earthquakes and probably by Merapi's eruptions, it lay in ruins for centuries, and reconstruction only really began in the twentieth century, piece by numbered piece. The 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake damaged it again, and repairs went on for years. Around the main group lie other temples worth seeing, including Sewu, a large Buddhist complex just to the north, a reminder that the Hindu and Buddhist dynasties of Central Java built side by side. In the dry season, the Ramayana ballet is performed on an open-air stage with the floodlit towers behind.

For riders, this is scooter country, and the main road between Yogya and Solo is busy, fast and chaotic, with buses, trucks and swarms of motorbikes all jostling for space. Ride defensively, keep a steady line and use the horn as locals do, as a friendly announcement rather than an insult. The smaller roads north towards the slopes of Merapi are far more pleasant, climbing through rice fields, villages and salak palm plantations into cooler air, with the volcano looming larger as you go.

Candi Prambanan and the surrounding towns are densely populated, so fuel is easy: Pertamina stations are common, and in villages you will see petrol sold in glass bottles at roadside stalls. Warungs everywhere sell nasi goreng, gudeg, the sweet jackfruit stew Yogyakarta is famous for, and cold drinks. Go early in the morning, both for cooler riding and for the light on the towers, and bring a sarong or cover-up for the temple grounds. Afternoon thunderstorms in the wet season can be torrential.
t.site of han gu pass of han dynasty in xi:
The Hangu Pass is one of the legendary places of Chinese history. According to tradition, it was at the old Hangu Pass, guarding the narrow road between the Central Plain and the Wei valley, that the philosopher Laozi, leaving China on the back of an ox, was asked by the gatekeeper to write down his wisdom before passing, and the result was the Tao Te Ching. That pass lies further west, near Lingbao. In 114 BC, under the Han dynasty, the pass was moved east to Xin'an county, near Luoyang, and it is the remains of this later Han pass, with its gate, walls and stretches of ancient road, that form part of the Silk Roads World Heritage site, on the route between the capitals of Chang'an and Luoyang and on towards Central Asia.

The landscape here is the loess country of western Henan: yellow earth hills cut by deep gullies, terraced fields of wheat and maize, villages of brick and earth, and the Yellow River flowing not far to the north. In spring, the hills turn green and fruit trees blossom, and in summer the heat can be intense. Luoyang, to the east, was the capital of several dynasties and is famous for the Longmen Grottoes, thousands of Buddhist caves and statues carved into the cliffs along the Yi River, and for the White Horse Temple, said to be the first Buddhist temple in China. In April, the city celebrates its famous peonies with a festival.

Riding in China presents particular challenges for foreigners. International driving permits are not recognised, so a Chinese licence and registered vehicle are required, and many cities restrict or ban motorcycles in their central areas. Expressways are generally closed to motorcycles. On the national and provincial roads, traffic is mixed and unpredictable, with trucks, buses, electric scooters, tricycles and pedestrians. The roads through the loess hills can be dusty in dry weather and muddy in the rain.

Yima and Xin'an have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Luoyang, about twenty-five kilometres away, is a large city with everything you need. Try the Luoyang water banquet, a series of soups and stews served one after the other, and the local noodles, and do not miss the Longmen Grottoes at sunset.
t.historic monuments of dengfeng in the ce:
The Dengfeng monuments are scattered along the southern foot of Mount Song, one of China's five sacred mountains, in the middle of Henan province. UNESCO grouped them together because they trace three thousand years of people treating one mountain as the centre of the world.

Its curving profile looks oddly modern, almost like a rocket ship made of clay. Shaolin gets the crowds because of the martial arts and the films, but the buildings that survive there are mostly later than its reputation, and the pagoda forest, where abbots are commemorated in stone, is quieter and more affecting than the training displays. A little further on is the Zhou Gong observatory platform at Gaocheng, a simple stone gnomon on a terrace where astronomers measured the midsummer shadow to fix the middle of the earth. Dengfeng was literally the place from which the empire calculated its calendar.

The surrounding country is dry, loess-tinged farmland that climbs sharply into grey rock ridges, and the smell in the morning is of woodsmoke, incense and wet stone. Roads around the ticketed sites are busy with tour buses and delivery trucks, so go early, before the groups arrive, and expect plenty of junctions, speed enforcement and local traffic habits that need patience. Motorcycle rules in Chinese cities and scenic areas vary by place and can be strict, so check what is allowed on a foreign-plated or hired machine well before you plan to ride here; it is not somewhere to improvise.

Songyang has fuel, restaurants and hotels in quantity, and Zhengzhou is the big city a couple of hours away if you need anything serious. Spring and autumn are the comfortable seasons. Summer is hot and hazy, and the winter mornings bite. Whatever the timing, leave an afternoon for slowing down, because the sites are spread out and each rewards a bit of walking more than a quick photograph.
t.sangiran early man site@-7.4,110.8:
Half of what we know about Homo erectus in Asia seems to have come out of the ground near this village in central Java. Sangiran is a dome of eroded earth, a few kilometres across, in which stream cuts have exposed layers of volcanic ash and river sediment that built up over about two million years, and in those layers the bones of early humans and extinct animals have turned up. The first finds were made in the 1930s, notably by the German palaeontologist Ralph von Koenigswald, and the site has since produced the remains of some fifty individuals, about half of all known fossils of its kind in the world. UNESCO listed it in 1996.

You arrive across the flat, fertile plain of the Solo river, where rice fields, sugarcane and small brick-making yards stretch in every direction, and the dark cone of Mount Lawu stands on the horizon. Riding in Java is a lesson in patience and attention. Roads are crowded with motorbikes, lorries and minibuses, drivers overtake in unexpected places, and dogs, chickens and children appear at the roadside. Traffic drives on the left. The heat is steady all year, with the dry season from roughly May to September offering the clearest days, and the rains, from November to March, bringing sudden downpours that flood low sections.

Fuel is no problem, since Indonesian petrol stations and roadside vendors are everywhere. Colomadu, about seventeen kilometres away, has over twenty-six thousand people, and Surakarta, known as Solo, is a city of more than half a million, with a royal palace, batik markets and a famous street food scene. Try the local rice dishes, sweet soups and the soft, spicy sauces that Javanese cooking favours.

The museum at Sangiran displays some of the finds, and the viewing tower looks out across the exposed hills. Walk the paths carefully, because the soil is loose and crumbly, and remember that the site is protected. To stand above the excavations and think of the people who lived here a million years ago is a humbling thing, especially on a hazy afternoon when the plain below seems to go on forever.
t.taishi que gates@34.5,113.1:
At the foot of Mount Song, one of the five sacred mountains of China, stand three pairs of free-standing stone gateways that have been waiting for the better part of two thousand years. They are que, tall, pillar-like towers that marked the approach to a temple or tomb in Han dynasty China, and the ones at Dengfeng belong to the temples of Mount Song, as ceremonial entrance markers. The Taishi Que, the western gate of the Zhongyue Temple, dates from the second century, and is covered with carved scenes of hunting, chariots, dancers and animals, in a lively, rough, vigorous style. They are among the oldest such structures in China and they are part of the UNESCO listing of the Historic Monuments of Dengfeng.

Mount Song also holds the Shaolin Monastery, the birthplace of Chan Buddhism and of the martial arts that carry its name, the Songyue Pagoda, a twelve-sided brick tower from the early sixth century, and the Songyang Academy. The wider landscape is of limestone ridges, terraces of persimmon and walnut trees, and loess hills, with the Yellow River basin to the north and the Central Plain stretching toward Luoyang and Zhengzhou.

Riding is possible in principle but practically difficult for foreign visitors. China requires a local licence, registration and a permit for foreign vehicles, and most travellers hire a car with a driver instead. The roads around Dengfeng are good, with roundabouts and busy traffic, and when you reach the mountain the roads climb in bends through villages and woods. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summer is hot with thunderstorms, and winter can bring snow and cold wind. Weekends and national holidays are crowded, particularly around Shaolin, so a weekday morning is better.

Songyang, a few kilometres away, is a town of sixty thousand with fuel, hotels and lots of restaurants and martial arts schools. Henan cuisine is noodle-heavy, so try hand-pulled noodles, steamed buns and braised lamb. Tickets for the sights are sold separately or in combination, and the gates themselves are fenced, so you see them from a short distance. Wear shoes with good grip for the stone steps, and take water in summer, since the sun is hot and shade is scarce around the monuments.
t.songyang academy of classical learning@3:
Long before there were universities in Europe, Chinese scholars gathered at academies in quiet places to read, argue and teach, and the Songyang Academy at the foot of Mount Song was one of the four great ones of the Song dynasty. It began life as a Buddhist temple and a Daoist retreat, and in the eleventh century it was turned into a school. Its most famous teachers were the brothers Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, who helped shape the school of thought called Neo-Confucianism. The buildings you see today are mostly later rebuildings, in the Ming and Qing styles, with courtyards and halls in grey brick and tile.

The best thing about the Academy is its trees. Two ancient cypresses stand in the grounds, thick and gnarled, said to date from the Han dynasty or earlier, and the Emperor Wu of Han is said to have named them. Whether the legend is true, they are old, and their shapes are very beautiful in morning light. The academy is part of the Dengfeng monuments listed by UNESCO, together with the Shaolin Monastery, the Zhongyue Temple and the Han gates nearby.

The setting is typical for the Song mountains. Limestone slopes rise behind, planted with walnut and persimmon, and paths wind up into the hills to lookout points and small temples. The roads around Dengfeng are well paved, with tight bends as they climb toward the high villages, but foreign visitors face considerable hurdles to ride in China, with local licences, plates and permits required. Many people hire a driver or take the local buses. Spring and autumn give the clearest views. Summer brings heat and storms, and winter can be cold, with snow in the hills.

Songyang is a town of some sixty thousand people, only three kilometres away, with fuel, shops, small hotels and plenty of noodle restaurants. Try the local steamed buns, mutton soup and flat bread. The academy is quieter than neighbouring Shaolin, which gets thick crowds, so it makes an excellent early morning stop. Tickets are inexpensive, and combination tickets with other monuments are sometimes offered. Wear sturdy shoes for the paths and carry water.
t.huishan temple@34.5,113.0:
Dengfeng lies below Mount Song, one of the five sacred mountains of China, and the temples scattered at its foot make up one of the densest clusters of historic buildings in Henan. Huishan Temple is part of that cluster, and it is the kind of place that most visitors drive straight past on the way to the Shaolin monastery, which is a pity. It sits quietly on the edge of Songyang, a town of sixty thousand people only five kilometres away, and it rewards anyone who stops to look.

The story here is the story of the whole mountain. For well over a thousand years Song has been where emperors came to perform rites and where monks, Daoists and scholars set up their retreats. The listing of the Dengfeng monuments "in the centre of heaven and earth" recognises that this was believed to be the middle of the world, and Huishan is one of the buildings in that group. The temple's long history includes the usual cycle of building, decay and restoration, and what you see is the product of many hands.

The riding around the foot of Song is pleasant rather than dramatic. The road from Zhengzhou or Luoyang crosses loess hills and farm country, then climbs gently toward the ridge, where the limestone and sandstone cliffs of the mountain suddenly show above the fields. There are decent corners on the approaches and enough variation to keep it interesting, but expect heavy traffic near the main tourist sites, and be careful about buses and tour coaches, which are not shy about the centre line.

Fuel and food are simple here. Songyang and Dengfeng have petrol stations and plenty of restaurants, and Zijinglu to the east is bigger still. Local noodles, steamed buns and the soups of Henan are good, honest fuel for a rider, and spring and autumn are the easiest seasons because summer can be hot and the winter wind off the mountain bites.

This particular stop is linked on the ride with the Longmen Grottoes and the Han-dynasty pass site, which shows how much history is packed into this one province. Take your time, because the temple is small and the hill behind it invites a short walk.
t.songye temple pagoda@34.5,113.0:
The Songyue pagoda is the one that any historian of Chinese architecture will point you toward, and it stands in the grounds of an old temple at the foot of Mount Song, five kilometres from Songyang. It is a tall brick pagoda with twelve sides, a shape found almost nowhere else, rising in tiers of tightly packed eaves to a slender top. By most accounts it dates from the early sixth century, which makes it the oldest brick pagoda in China, and one of the oldest standing buildings in the country.

What strikes you first is how well it has aged. The brick has the colour of old ivory in sunlight and a rich brown when the weather is wet, and the outline is clean and confident. Inside, the hollow shaft rises through the whole structure. It is part of the group of monuments around Dengfeng that UNESCO has recognised as the centre of heaven and earth, a title that sounds grandiose but reflects how central Song was to Chinese religious life.

Getting here is easy enough. The road from Zhengzhou runs south-west through the loess hills and farmland of Henan, then picks up the line of the Song range, whose limestone ridges appear suddenly above the fields. The bends are not tight but they come regularly, and a few climbs give you a view of the valley behind. Traffic is busy near Dengfeng itself, especially at weekends and public holidays, when coaches fill the parking lots near Shaolin. Go early on a weekday and you will have a very different experience.

Songyang and Dengfeng have all the fuel, food and beds you could want, with plenty of noodle shops and small restaurants serving the soups and breads of the Central Plains. Zijinglu, a larger town nearby, has more still. Spring and autumn are best for riding, while summer can be hot and winter windy.

This stop is paired on the ride with the Longmen Grottoes and with the Han Gu Pass site, and the three together give a very good picture of how thickly layered the history of Henan is. Stand a minute at the base of the pagoda and look up, because most visitors just take a photo and leave.
t.borobudur temple@-7.6,110.2:
Borobudur rises out of the Kedu Plain in central Java like a mountain that someone has carved into a book. Built in the ninth century under the Sailendra dynasty, it is the largest Buddhist monument in the world, a stepped pyramid of volcanic stone that stands about thirty metres high, with nine platforms, six square and three round, crowned by a central stupa. Walking up the galleries, you pass nearly three thousand relief panels telling the story of the Buddha's lives and the path to enlightenment, and as you reach the upper terraces, seventy-two perforated stupas hold seated Buddha figures looking out across the fields toward the volcanoes.

For several centuries the monument was abandoned, and it was eventually covered by ash, vegetation and soil, partly hidden from the world until it was brought back to attention in the early nineteenth century during the British interregnum under Thomas Stamford Raffles. A major restoration with UNESCO support in the 1970s took the whole structure apart and rebuilt it with new drainage. The volcano Merapi, which looms to the north-east, covered the area in ash in the eruption of 2010, and locals still live with the mountain as a neighbour.

Riding here is a very different business from the mountain roads in other parts of Java. The roads between Yogyakarta and Magelang are busy with scooters, trucks and buses, and the pace is stop-and-go with constant little overtaking manoeuvres. The tarmac is mostly good, but you need to ride defensively, expect the unexpected and give way to everything larger than you. Go early, as the heat builds quickly, and the afternoon sun is hard on the stone, which is why the temple opens at dawn. Mertoyudan and Muntilan, the two nearby towns, offer fuel, food stalls and a wide range of simple hotels, so there is no shortage of services.

Visitor numbers to the upper levels are limited, with timed tickets and special footwear provided, so check the current rules online before arriving. Sunrise views from a nearby hill are famous, and on a misty morning the temple appears to float on a sea of cloud, a sight that makes the early alarm entirely worthwhile.

Eat gudeg, a sweet jackfruit stew from Yogyakarta, or the fried chicken and sambal sold by roadside vendors, and drink sweet iced tea. A Javanese afternoon can be slow, and the best response is to match it.
t.borobudur temple compounds@-7.6,110.2:
The name Compounds is the clue to what makes this place unusual: Borobudur is not alone. The monument forms part of a larger sacred landscape in the Kedu Plain, where the river Progo and the river Elo meet, a setting that Javanese tradition regarded as a spiritual centre. Two smaller temples, Pawon and Mendut, stand to the east of the main monument in a straight line, and the three together were included in the UNESCO listing. Archaeologists still argue over exactly why they were aligned that way, but the idea that pilgrims once walked between them as part of a ritual route is widely accepted.

This part of Java is one of the most fertile places in Asia. Volcanic ash from Merapi and Merbabu, the neighbouring peaks, has enriched the soil for thousands of years, and the plain is a patchwork of rice paddies, tobacco, chilli and banana plants, with coconut palms along the lanes. Seen from the upper terraces, the fields shine green after rain, the mountains stand behind them, and the whole scene feels as if the temple has been dropped into a garden.

For the rider, the back lanes around the temple are far nicer than the main highway. They run along irrigation canals and between rice fields, narrow and often shared with bicycles, ox carts, schoolchildren and ducks, and the speed limit is whatever the smallest vehicle can manage. Surfaces are generally smooth but can be slippery with mud and wet leaves, and it is wise to carry cash for small purchases, since cards are not widely accepted off the main roads. Petrol can be found in Muntilan and Mertoyudan, both large towns with several stations, and in many villages roadside stalls sell bottled fuel.

The dry season, from roughly May to September, is the best time for a visit, with clearer skies and less mud. The rainy season fills the sky with dramatic cloud and brings a steady heat, and Merapi sometimes hides itself completely behind the weather.

Take a break in a village, buy a cup of coffee from a stall and watch life pass by. You will probably be offered snacks, asked where you are from and asked for a photo, in a friendly way that can quickly become the best part of the day.
t.pawon temple@-7.6,110.2:
Pawon is the small one, and I have a soft spot for it. While Borobudur is huge and Mendut grand, Pawon is a compact stone temple about two kilometres from Borobudur, set in a quiet garden among village houses. It looks like a miniature tower, with a carved doorway, a tiered roof and relief carvings of trees and mythical beings on the outer walls, and inside, the chamber is almost empty. Scholars still debate what it was for, with one idea being that it was a place where pilgrims purified themselves before continuing to the larger temple, and another that it was linked to a royal figure.

Each year at the Buddhist festival of Vesak, monks and pilgrims walk in procession from Mendut through Pawon to Borobudur, a route of a few kilometres that connects the three temples in a single ritual. That walk gives the place a living significance, and if your plans match the full moon of May or thereabouts, you might witness it, though the crowds will be large and roads closed.

The riding here is all about small roads. From Muntilan, a busy market town with petrol, supermarkets and plenty of warungs, you ride east through villages, past brick kilns and stalls selling fruit and snacks, with Merapi on the skyline when the cloud lifts. Do not expect corners, since the Kedu Plain is mostly flat, but the traffic can be chaotic and the potholes are real. Scooters turn without signalling, chickens cross the road, and children wave from the doorways. It is best to ride slowly and keep your eyes peeled.

Because Pawon is so small, a visit takes only ten or fifteen minutes, which makes it a good stop between the larger monuments. There is a small charge at some times of year and opening hours are set, so a little checking beforehand helps. Local guides offer to show you around, and a small tip is appreciated if you accept.

The pleasure of Pawon is that you can still hear birdsong and the swish of a broom in a nearby yard, which is something rare on the tourist trail. The air smells of woodsmoke, frangipani and diesel, in roughly that order.
t.shark bay@-25.9,113.5:
The bay is a huge, shallow, salty inlet of the Indian Ocean, and it holds the largest seagrass meadows in the world, which feed a population of dugongs, turtles and dolphins. The water is clear, the sand is white and the cliffs are red.

Several remarkable things sit in a short distance. At Monkey Mia, a beach not far from Denham, wild bottlenose dolphins swim into the shallows each morning to be fed by rangers, a tradition that began informally decades ago and now follows strict rules. At Hamelin Pool, the water is twice as salty as the sea, and it hosts stromatolites, rounded mounds built by microbes, which are living relatives of some of the oldest life forms on Earth. At Shell Beach, the sand is made up of billions of tiny white cockle shells, stacked metres deep for many kilometres.

The history is old and thin. In 1616 the Dutch captain Dirk Hartog landed on an island at the mouth of the bay and nailed a pewter plate to a post, the first recorded European landing on the Australian coast, and the island now carries his name. Pearling, fishing and salt have kept the area alive since. The Francois Peron National Park, on the peninsula north of Denham, has red dunes, white beaches and blue water, though much of it needs a four-wheel drive to explore.

For the rider, the road to Denham is a long spur of more than a hundred kilometres off the North West Coastal Highway, running through low scrub and past salt pans, and it ends at the sea. Distances between fuel stops are long, so Denham has a station and basic supplies, and it is wise to fill up there. Wind is often strong, and the heat is fierce in summer.

Pack plenty of water, sunscreen and a hat. A swim in the clear water, a plate of fresh fish and an evening on the jetty, watching the sky turn pink, will reward the long road.
t.watson lake@60.1,-128.7:
Watson Lake is a small town in the southern Yukon, at the junction of the Alaska Highway and the road to the Cassiar country, and it is famous for one very odd thing: a forest of signs. In 1942, during the building of the highway, a homesick American soldier named Carl Lindley put up a sign pointing to his home town in Illinois, and others followed. Today there are more than a hundred thousand signs, licence plates and street signs from all over the world, nailed to posts in a field beside the road. People still bring their own, and a visitor centre helps you find a place to hang it.

The Alaska Highway itself was a wartime project, built in 1942 by American army engineers and civilian contractors in about eight months, to link the lower forty-eight to Alaska after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Watson Lake had an airfield, part of a chain of fields used to ferry aircraft to the Soviet Union, and the town grew around it. The surrounding country is boreal forest, lakes and low mountains, with the Liard River winding nearby, and the light in summer lasts nearly all night.

For a rider, the highway through here is a long, straight, heavy-traffic ribbon, mostly paved but with sections of frost heave, patched surface and loose gravel. Rain is common, and the road can be slick, so allow plenty of time. Wildlife is part of the journey: bison, black bears, moose and caribou wander onto the road, and the large animals are a real danger at dawn and dusk. Mosquitoes in summer can be fierce, and a head net is handy at stops. The summer weather is warm and long, but temperatures can drop sharply at night.

The town, with around fifteen hundred people, has fuel, food and a few motels, and it is the place to fill up, since distances between services on the highway are large, often a couple of hundred kilometres. Liard Hot Springs, a pleasant natural pool in a forest setting, lies some distance to the east, and it is a good place to soak after a long day in the saddle. Westward lies Whitehorse, a long day's ride away. Stop for coffee in town, hang a sign if you have one, and check your tyre pressures before going on.
t.yogyakarta@-7.8,110.4:
Yogyakarta is the cultural heart of Java, and it still has a living sultan. The Kraton, the sultan's palace, stands at the centre of the city, surrounded by courtyards, pavilions and a walled quarter, and the ruling sultan serves as the governor of the special region, a unique arrangement in Indonesia. The city is also a university town, full of students, art, batik workshops and a famous street, Malioboro, that fills with food stalls and horse-drawn carts in the evening.

To the north, the volcano Merapi, nearly three thousand metres high and one of the most active in Indonesia, hangs over the city and often puffs steam. Its eruptions have shaped the land and the lives of the people for centuries. In the plain around, the fields are rice, with palms and banana trees, and the soil is rich with volcanic ash. The great Buddhist monument of Borobudur, built in the ninth century, stands about forty kilometres to the north-west, and the Hindu temples of Prambanan lie to the east. Pawon, a small temple of brick-red volcanic stone, stands in a line between Borobudur and Mendut and is thought to have been part of a ritual path.

Riding in Java is an adventure of scale. Scooters swarm, buses roar, and everything seems to move at once, yet there is an unspoken order, and traffic flows. Traffic drives on the left. The best advice is to stay calm, ride predictably and give way to larger vehicles. Roads in the countryside are narrower and beautiful, with smooth stretches and unexpected potholes. In the rainy season, from roughly November to March, afternoon downpours are heavy, and the dry months of May to September offer the clearest weather.

Fuel is on sale everywhere, from official stations to roadside stalls, and the food is superb. Try gudeg, a sweet jackfruit stew with rice, eggs and chicken, which is the signature dish of the city, and sip strong sweet tea or coffee. Wear a helmet, carry your papers and respect the customs at temples, where shoulders and knees should be covered. An early start in the cool of the morning is the best way to see the monuments before the heat and the crowds.
t.bromo tengger scenic road point 3@-8.0,1:
At around 2,400 metres, the road from Malang over the Tengger massif reaches the rim of one of the most extraordinary landscapes in Indonesia. From here, at the southern edge of the great caldera, you look down into a vast, flat plain of volcanic sand, the Sea of Sand, with the smoking cone of Bromo rising from it and, beyond, the perfect cone of Semeru, the highest mountain on Java at 3,676 metres, puffing out regular plumes of ash. It is a view that makes people stop talking.

The Tengger caldera is about ten kilometres across, the remains of an ancient volcano that collapsed after a massive eruption, and inside it new cones have grown, including Bromo, Batok and others. The whole area is part of the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park, which also protects forests, lakes and the slopes of Semeru. Just below the rim on this side lie grassy hills and valleys, green and soft after the rains, known locally as the Teletubbies hills, and a savanna where horses graze.

The Tengger people, who live in villages around the caldera, are one of the few Hindu communities on Java, descendants, according to legend, of Majapahit nobles who fled to the mountains when Islam spread across the island. They farm the steep slopes, growing potatoes, cabbages and onions, and they hold Bromo sacred, making offerings to the volcano during the annual Yadnya Kasada festival. Their villages are built of wood and brick, with bright painted doors, and the people wear sarongs wrapped around their shoulders against the cold.
