The road up from Malang through Tumpang is steep, narrow and winding, with a rough surface in places and very tight hairpins near the top. It is popular with riders, and with jeeps carrying tourists, so expect traffic, especially at weekends. The descent into the Sea of Sand is on a steep, sometimes sandy track, and riding on the sand itself requires skill and confidence. There are no services on the rim, so fill up in Tumpang or Malang, and dress for winter, because it is cold at this altitude, especially before dawn. Sunrise and early morning offer the best light and clearest views.
t.bromo tengger scenic road point 4@-7.9,1:
Down on the floor of the Tengger caldera, the Sea of Sand stretches away in every direction, a grey-black plain of fine volcanic ash surrounded by cliffs, with Bromo smoking at its centre. It is a strange, otherworldly place: silent except for the wind and the roar of jeep engines, with dust devils swirling across the plain and a Hindu temple, Pura Luhur Poten, standing alone at the foot of Bromo like something from a dream. In the early morning, mist fills the caldera, and the cones rise out of it like islands.

Bromo itself is an active volcano, with a crater that pours out white sulphurous smoke and occasionally ash. A staircase of more than two hundred steps leads up the side of the cone to the crater rim, where you can look down into the steaming vent, with the smell of sulphur strong and the roar of the gas loud. During the Yadnya Kasada festival, the Tengger people climb to the rim and throw offerings of vegetables, chickens and money into the crater to appease the gods, while local men try to catch the offerings on the slopes below.

The volcano is regularly active, and authorities sometimes close the crater area or the whole caldera when activity increases, so check the current status before you go. The ash and sand can be a problem for vehicles, getting into engines and brakes, and for riders' eyes and lungs, so bring goggles and a mask or scarf. Horses can be hired to carry visitors across the sand to the foot of the cone.

Riding on the Sea of Sand is a challenge. The sand is soft and deep in places, and the tracks are rutted by jeeps, so it is easy to get stuck or drop the bike. It is best done on a lightweight bike with knobbly tyres, or not at all if you are not confident on loose surfaces. There are no services in the caldera, and the nearest fuel is in the villages on the rim or in the towns below. Mornings beat afternoons, before the wind lifts the ash, and May to October is the most reliable season.
t.bromo tengger scenic road point 5@-7.9,1:
Cemoro Lawang is the village perched on the north-eastern rim of the Tengger caldera, and for most visitors it is the gateway to Bromo. It is a small place, with a single main street lined with guesthouses, warungs and shops selling warm hats and gloves, and the houses cling to the edge of the cliff, looking down into the Sea of Sand. At dawn, the village comes alive with jeeps and motorbikes heading for the viewpoints, and by mid-morning it is quiet again, as visitors return to bed or move on.

The classic view of Bromo is from the viewpoint at Penanjakan, a peak on the rim a few kilometres from the village, where crowds gather before dawn to watch the sun rise over the caldera. As the light grows, the cones of Bromo, Batok and Semeru emerge from the mist, and the colours change from purple to pink to gold. It is one of the most famous sunrises in Indonesia, and on a clear morning it lives up to its reputation, though the crowds can be large and the jostling for position intense. Quieter viewpoints along the rim offer similar views with fewer people.

The village is home to Tengger people, and the farms around it grow vegetables on terraced slopes so steep it seems impossible to work them. Life here is hard, with cold nights and frequent fog, and tourism has become an important source of income. The local food is simple: rice, vegetables, fried tempeh, and hot sweet tea or coffee, which tastes wonderful in the cold morning air.

The road from Cemoro Lawang down to Probolinggo, on the north coast of Java, is a long, steep descent through farmland and forest, with hairpin bends and sweeping curves. Trucks and buses share the asphalt, and your brakes will be warm by the bottom. Pasuruan, about thirty kilometres away, and Probolinggo are the nearest large towns with full services, though there is fuel in the villages on the way. The weather at Cemoro Lawang is cool to cold, and fog can roll in at any time, so pack waterproofs and a warm layer, and aim to arrive in daylight.
